content: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO) is a frequent condition in infants that leads to excessive tearing during the first year of life. This condition arises due to a blockage in the nasolacrimal duct system, which can result in symptoms such as excessive tearing or mucoid discharge from the eyes. The obstruction may also cause skin maceration around the eyelids and increase the risk of local infections, such as conjunctivitis, which may necessitate antibiotic treatment. The prevalence of NLDO in early childhood is estimated to range between 5% and 20%, and in many cases, the condition resolves spontaneously without surgical intervention. Management of NLDO includes both conservative and surgical approaches. Conservative treatments involve observation, massage of the lacrimal sac, and the use of antibiotics. Alternatively, probing of the nasolacrimal duct can be performed to address the membranous obstruction at the distal end of the duct. Probing may be conducted in an office setting without anesthesia or in an operating room under general anesthesia. This procedure aims to alleviate symptoms by opening the obstruction. However, probing may fail in cases where the obstruction is caused by a bony protrusion of the inferior turbinate into the duct or when the duct is swollen due to infection, such as dacryocystitis. Potential complications of probing include the creation of a false passage, injury to the nasolacrimal duct, canaliculi, or puncta, bleeding, laryngospasm, or aspiration. To evaluate the effectiveness of probing for congenital NLDO, a systematic review was conducted. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing immediate probing (performed in an office or hospital setting) with deferred probing or other non-surgical interventions, such as observation, antibiotic drops, or antibiotic drops combined with massage. The studies included children aged three weeks to four years who presented with symptoms of tearing and conjunctivitis. Data were analyzed using Review Manager software, and the certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Two RCTs were identified, involving a total of 303 eyes from 242 participants with either unilateral or bilateral NLDO. In both studies, immediate office-based probing was compared to deferred probing, which was performed after six months of observation or when the child reached a specific age. The primary outcome, treatment success at six months, was partially reported in one study. In the deferred probing group, 66% of eyes (77 out of 117) resolved without surgery after six months, while 34% (40 eyes) did not resolve and required probing. Among children with unilateral NLDO, those who underwent immediate probing had a higher likelihood of treatment success compared to those in the deferred probing group (relative risk [RR] 1.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.12 to 1.78; moderate-certainty evidence). Treatment success for all children was assessed at 18 months in one study. Results were analyzed separately for unilateral and bilateral NLDO. For unilateral NLDO, the relative risk of treatment success was 1.13 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.28), while for bilateral NLDO, the relative risk was 0.86 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.06). However, the evidence for these outcomes was of very low certainty. In a smaller study involving 26 eyes from 22 children, immediate probing resulted in a higher cure rate within one month compared to deferred probing, with results analyzed at 15 months (RR 2.56, 95% CI 1.16 to 5.64). The evidence from this study was considered low-certainty due to the small sample size and concerns about attrition bias. One study reported the need for reoperation, but data were only available for the immediate probing group. Secondary procedures were required in 9% of children with unilateral NLDO and 13% of those with bilateral NLDO. Cost-effectiveness was also assessed in one study, which found that the mean cost of immediate probing was lower than that of deferred probing. However, the cost difference was uncertain (mean difference USD -139, 95% CI USD -377 to 94; moderate-certainty evidence). Reported complications from probing were not serious. One study noted no complications or serious adverse events, while the other reported bleeding from the punctum in 20% of all probings. In conclusion, the effects and costs of immediate versus deferred probing for NLDO remain uncertain. Immediate office-based probing may offer better outcomes for children with unilateral NLDO, but the evidence is limited due to the small number of participants and variability in outcome assessment time points. Further research, including larger and more robust clinical trials, is needed to determine the optimal timing and effectiveness of probing for NLDO.
